claims.text: The Z method can be used with ab initio molecular dynamics to estimate melting temperature.
The Z method can estimate entropy and enthalpy of fusion and volume change at melting.
The Z method is more computationally efficient than full thermodynamic integration.
The simulated material initially has a perfect crystalline structure at zero pressure.
Under the Z-method protocol, the crystalline system is superheated until it melts spontaneously.
The simulations are conducted at constant volume in the NVE ensemble.
A sufficiently large simulation cell is required to capture nucleation effects.
Melting produces a transition from crystalline order to a disordered liquid state.
The Z method uses the energy-temperature trajectory of a superheated solid.
When internal energy exceeds a critical value, the superheated solid melts abruptly.
The melting temperature can be inferred from the abrupt melting event.
Entropy, enthalpy, and volume changes can be derived from sudden changes in thermodynamic observables at the transition.
The simulation will identify a well-defined energy threshold for melting.
Z-method melting-temperature estimates will agree with results from thermodynamic integration.
Thermodynamic integration has a much higher computational cost than the Z method.
Small system size can limit the efficiency and accuracy of the Z method.
Strong anharmonic effects near melting can perturb the energy-temperature trajectory and limit accuracy.
Z-method results may be sensitive to simulation-cell size and boundary conditions.

contradictions.description: The proposed simulation is explicitly constant-volume, yet the mechanism and outcome imply that a volume change or volume jump at melting will be directly observed. A fixed-volume trajectory cannot itself exhibit a change in total simulation-cell volume; an additional volume-dependent or pressure-dependent calculation would need to be specified.
